extracted.intended_audience: seminarians, theology students, Catholic theologians, clergy
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Catholic dogmatic theology concerning sanctifying grace, the indwelling of the Holy Ghost, certainty of justification, increase and loss of grace, and the merit of good works. Intended as a systematic doctrinal treatment for students and scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between accidental and substantial indwelling of the Holy Ghost
rubrics_metrics.description: Holy Scripture draws a clear-cut distinction between the accidental and the substantial indwelling of the Holy Ghost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by Scriptural citations (e.g., John XIV; Romans; 1 Corinthians) and patristic testimony. The text treats this distinction as foundational for subsequent theological reflection on how the Holy Ghost 'abides' in the just (i.e., whether the presence is properly substantial/personal or only accidental/analogous).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal/substantial indwelling of the Holy Ghost in the just
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture and the Fathers teach that the Holy Ghost is given in Person to the faithful and abides in the just, so that their souls become temples of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by John XIV, Romans V and VIII, 1 Corinthians III and VI. Patristic witnesses (Athanasius, Basil, Cyril, Augustine) are cited to show the Fathers’ affirmation that the Holy Ghost's indwelling is personal and grounds theosis/deification of the believer. Use of patristic testimony is treated as authoritative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority account of manner of indwelling: Trinity's common indwelling appropriated to the Holy Ghost
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority view holds that the Holy Ghost does not dwell in the soul 'as the soul dwells in the body' nor by a hypostatic union; rather the indwelling is objectively an indwelling of the whole Trinity, appropriated to the Third Person because of his relation as 'hypostatic holiness' or 'personal love.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This account appeals to the 'fundamental law of the Trinity' (unity except where relations oppose) and Scriptural passages of mutual indwelling (e.g., John XIV, 23). It explains the indwelling as the state of grace bearing a special relation to the Third Person (appropriation), not as a physical or hypostatic union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative account of manner of indwelling: union of the Holy Ghost Himself with the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Some theologians (e.g., Petavius, Passaglia, Scheeben) argue that the Fathers conceived the indwelling as a unique union of the Holy Ghost Himself with the soul — neither physical nor hypostatic but a moral/accidental/active union directly uniting the person of the Holy Ghost to the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as an exalted/mystic theory; proponents are named. The text notes objections and tensions of this view with Trinitarian appropriations and missions, signaling it as an alternative but controversial interpretive model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property (proprium) — definition and distinction from accident
rubrics_metrics.description: A property is a quality that necessarily flows from the essence of a thing and is found in all individuals of the same species; it is opposed to an accident, which may or may not be present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: ability to laugh is a property of human nature, skin color is an accident. This ontological distinction is applied to clarify what counts as a necessary consequence of sanctifying grace versus what is incidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction among properties of grace, formal effects, and supernatural concomitants
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal effects of grace are the elements constituting its nature; properties are determinations necessarily flowing from that nature; supernatural concomitants are free gifts superadded by God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite distinction when classifying consequences of sanctifying grace: decide whether a given effect is constitutive (formal), necessarily consequent (property), or an extra gratuitous favor (concomitant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis I: No man knows with certainty of faith whether he is justified or not
rubrics_metrics.description: It is de fide that no one (without special revelation) can know with the certainty of faith that he is justified; certitudo fidei in oneself is rejected while humble trust (certitudo spei) is permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounds: Council of Trent’s rejection of 'fiduciary faith,' Scripture (Pauline warnings), and patristic testimony. Applied pastoral criteria: avoid 'inanis fiducia' (vain confidence); foster humility and fear. The text explains types of certainty (theological, metaphysical, moral) and why only moral certainty generally applies to most believers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of theological/metaphysical certainty of personal justification without private revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: Theologians (except rare exceptions) deny that anyone can be theologically or metaphysically certain of his justification without special/private revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: (1) Scripture and Tradition do not support such claims, (2) lack of objective criteria outside private revelation, (3) Council of Trent censured assertions that one may be absolutely certain. Only in rare, divinely-revealed cases could theological certainty be mandated to the individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral certainty and practical criteria for reasonable assurance of soul's state
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral certainty about one's justification admits degrees and may be very high; signs that may relieve unreasonable anxiety include a taste for spiritual things, contempt for earthly pleasures, zeal and perseverance in good, love of prayer and pious meditation, patience in suffering, devotion to the Blessed Virgin, frequent reception of the sacraments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral certainty is the ordinary form of assurance available to believers; baptized infants may have the highest moral certainty (subject to ordinary doubts about ministerial intent and validity). Use the listed spiritual indicators as prudential tests for pastoral consolation, not as metaphysical guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis II: Sanctifying grace admits of degrees and can be increased by good works
rubrics_metrics.description: It is de fide that sanctifying grace is not equal in all the justified and can be increased by good works; justification is not a once-for-all equal allotment but may grow (gratia prima vs gratia secunda).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural and conciliar support cited (e.g., Prov., 2 Pet., Trent). The Council of Trent affirms that the Holy Ghost distributes justice according to His will and man’s disposition and that faith cooperating with good works increases justification. Both ex opere operantis (cooperation) and ex opere operato (sacraments) are means of increase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of venial sin to sanctifying grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Venial sin does not destroy the state of sanctifying grace and therefore does not directly augment or diminish sanctifying grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venial sin weakens will-power and habitually predisposes to mortal sin but cannot by itself convert grace into loss; theological rationale and pastoral cautions given to avoid concluding that many venial sins could gradually equal a mortal sin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models of how sanctifying grace increases: intensio vs additio gradus
rubrics_metrics.description: Two scholastic accounts: some describe increase as 'maior radicatio in subiecto' (deeper rooting), others describe it as 'additio gradus ad gradum' (addition of degrees). Majority favors additio gradus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The increase is treated as a physical augmentation of a supernatural quality — analogous to the increase of light/heat. The additio model is preferred as more intelligible and consistent with Scripture/Tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase of grace correlates with increase of charity and infused moral virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Every increase or decrease of sanctifying grace entails a corresponding increase or decrease of theological charity; likewise for the infused moral virtues (charity and grace are inseparable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faith and hope are treated differently (may persist apart from charity); Suarez and others discuss nuanced cases, but the normative assertion is that charity and grace are essentially linked so their quantities rise and fall together, affecting future heavenly glory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits to increase of sanctifying grace under ordained divine power
rubrics_metrics.description: Though no intrinsic contradiction exists in allowing indefinite augmentation of grace, under God's ordained power increases are limited by the unique fullness of grace in Christ and the fullness granted to the Blessed Virgin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theological humility is advised — aim to approach these supremely high ideals though actual infinity of grace in creatures is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis III: Sanctifying grace is lost by mortal sin
rubrics_metrics.description: It is de fide that sanctifying grace can be lost by mortal sin; the Council of Trent condemns the opposite positions (that grace cannot be lost or that only unbelief can cause loss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural evidence (Ezekiel, Paul, Christ's warnings) and patristic/traditional practice (penitential discipline) justify the teaching. Venial sin distinguished: venial sins do not destroy state of grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of forfeiture: which supernatural concomitants are lost with sanctifying grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Theological charity (love) is substantially identical with sanctifying grace and is lost with it; the habitus of faith is not destroyed by mortal sin except by the sin of unbelief; hope likely survives though contested; infused moral virtues and the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost disappear with sanctifying grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: 'accessorium sequitur principale' — accessory follows the principal. The unanimous teaching is that virtues/gifts dependent on sanctifying grace cannot persist without it; faith and perhaps hope have a different status and can subsist as habits absent charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal fruit of justification: meritoriousness of good works
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal fruit of justification is that all good works performed in the state of sanctifying grace are meritorious (entitle the doer to reward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merit is defined theologically as that property of a good work which entitles the doer to a reward. The point is set in opposition to various Protestant denials and supported by Scripture, Tradition, and Council decrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of merit: condign (strict) vs congruous (quasi-) merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of theological merit are distinguished: (1) condign merit (meritum adaequatum sive de condigno) involves an equality between service and return measured by commutative justice and confers a strict claim to reward; (2) congruous merit (meritum inadaequatum sive de congruo) is an inadequate merit that entitles to reward on grounds of equity rather than strict justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theological distinction governs how one should speak of reward due to good works: whether strictly owed by commutative measure (condign) or fittingly given by God's mercy/equity (congruous). The treatise treats merit in the supernatural/theological sense only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciliar and patristic criteria on merit and grace preceding works
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church (Second Council of Orange, Fourth Lateran, Council of Trent) teaches that grace precedes good works, yet good works performed in grace deserve reward; earlier heresies that denied this (Jovinianism, some Reformers) have been condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conciliar formulations to adjudicate disputes about the causal role of grace versus human cooperation: grace is necessary and precedes, but human cooperation and works performed in grace genuinely merit reward according to Church doctrine.
